extracted.intended_audience: readers of Rabelais / readers of early-modern satire and humorous prose
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter from Rabelais's Pantagruel (satirical prose) containing comic episodes, mock-encyclopedic lists, and a few explicit aphorisms about how to pose problems and give answers. The text is literary and not an instructional rubric, but it includes a small number of prescriptive statements about clarity, brevity, and mode of answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of problems/questions
rubrics_metrics.description: "the Peripatetics have wisely made a rule that all problems, questions, and doubts which are offered to be solved ought to be certain, clear, and intelligible."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page gives the rule and an immediate illustrative exchange: when Ponocrates asks about 'dog-sleep' Pantagruel requests clarification — Ponocrates explains he means 'to sleep fasting in the sun at noonday, as the dogs do.' The surrounding text implies that vague or ill-defined questions must be made precise before meaningful answers can be given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity and avoidance of pedantry in answers
rubrics_metrics.description: "My answer shall be short, not to tire you with a long needless train of pedantic cant."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pantagruel declares answers should be concise. The passage also contrasts verbal answers with actions: 'The belly has no ears, nor is it to be filled with fair words; you shall be answered to content by signs and gestures.' The Tarquin anecdote (answer by cutting tall poppies) is presented as an example of using a short, direct, nonverbal response rather than extended speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the appropriate mode of response — adapt medium to audience
rubrics_metrics.description: "The belly has no ears, nor is it to be filled with fair words; you shall be answered to content by signs and gestures."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prescriptive remark advises tailoring the mode of communication to the recipient (e.g., nonverbal signs for someone who 'does not hear' or will not be moved by words). The text immediately demonstrates this by Pantagruel pulling a bell-string and sending a practical signal (Friar John goes to the cook-room), and by the Tarquin/Gabii story showing symbolic nonverbal messaging as effective.
